title: Constant-Factor Approximation for Scheduling with Uniform Communication Delays
short_statement: Does $P\mid prec,c\mid C_{\max}$ admit a polynomial-time constant-factor approximation independent of the number of machines and the delay $c$?
open_problem: Find a polynomial-time constant-factor approximation for $P\mid prec,c\mid C_{\max}$ with uniform communication delay, or prove that no such approximation exists under a standard complexity assumption.
background: Communication-delay scheduling models parallel computation and distributed production systems in which a successor task can start quickly if it stays on the same processor but must wait if intermediate data, materials, or setup information crosses processors. This is a natural extension of precedence-constrained scheduling, but the delay constraint couples assignment and sequencing in a way that breaks many classical list-scheduling arguments. The problem appears in longstanding scheduling open-problem lists, including the Schuurman-Woeginger list and later updates discussed by Bansal and subsequent approximation papers. It is attractive for the ORdos collection because the model is extremely crisp: a precedence DAG, identical machines, and one scalar delay. The difficulty lies not in modeling but in finding an approximation method that avoids paying a factor growing with $c$ or $m$.
full_statement: An instance consists of jobs $J$ with processing times, $m$ identical parallel machines, a precedence DAG on $J$, and a uniform communication delay $c\ge 0$. A nonpreemptive schedule assigns each job to a machine and start time. If $i\prec j$ and $i,j$ are scheduled on the same machine, then $j$ may start after $i$ completes; if they are scheduled on different machines, then $j$ may start only at least $c$ time units after $i$ completes. The objective is to minimize $C_{\max}$. The open problem is whether there is a polynomial-time $O(1)$-approximation for $P\mid prec,c\mid C_{\max}$, where the approximation factor is independent of $m$, $n$, and $c$. A stronger resolution would identify the correct asymptotic approximability, perhaps matching a hardness threshold.
known_results: Graham-style list scheduling gives factors that grow with the communication delay. Davies, Kulkarni, Rothvoss, Tarnawski, and Zhang gave a polynomial-time $O(\log c\cdot \log m)$ approximation using Sherali-Adams liftings and randomized clustering, a major improvement over delay-linear bounds but still not constant. For non-uniform communication delays, Davies, Kulkarni, Rothvoss, Sandeep, Tarnawski, and Zhang proved logarithmic hardness under standard quasi-polynomial-time assumptions, showing that the broader delay model cannot have the same constant-factor behavior. Kulkarni, Li, Tarnawski, and Ye developed hierarchy-based algorithms for related precedence and communication-constrained settings. As of the 2026 check, the uniform-delay constant-factor question remains the clean unresolved target.

progress.summary: The best source-checked guarantee here is polylogarithmic in $c$ and $m$ for uniform delays. Non-uniform delays have logarithmic hardness, so the uniform case is the meaningful remaining constant-factor target.

counterexample_rationale: Lower bounds and integrality-gap examples may be expressible as finite precedence DAGs with delay values, so computational search could help. A full impossibility result would still need a complexity-theoretic reduction.
alphaevolve_rationale: Search can test LP gaps, clustering failures, and small hard precedence structures. It may also suggest rounding rules that beat known logarithmic dependence.

literature.synthesis: The central line of progress uses lift-and-round methods: a Sherali-Adams solution induces a semimetric over jobs, and randomized clustering turns fractional precedence/assignment information into a schedule. This yields $O(\log c\log m)$, which is qualitatively different from old delay-linear guarantees but still falls short of the open constant factor. The non-uniform-delay hardness paper clarifies that arbitrary edge delays are substantially harder and introduces UMPS as a hardness engine. That negative result sharpens the uniform-delay problem rather than resolving it: the remaining question is whether a single common delay contains enough structure for constant approximation, or whether a different hardness construction can survive the uniformity constraint.

agent_guidance.suitable_approaches: Study whether the clustering analysis can be made scale-free when all delays are equal, perhaps by replacing general metric decompositions with precedence-aware decompositions. Search for integrality gaps of natural time-indexed and hierarchy relaxations with small $c$ and $m$. A hardness route should try to encode UMPS-like structure while forcing all communication delays to be identical.
agent_guidance.verification_notes: A claimed algorithm must have a factor bounded by an absolute constant and run in polynomial time for arbitrary $m,c,n$. A claimed lower bound must apply to the uniform-delay model, not just the non-uniform model already known to be harder.

where_posed.text: Restated as an outstanding Schuurman-Woeginger/Bansal open problem in Davies et al., 'Scheduling with Communication Delays via LP Hierarchies and Clustering'.
